A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with matching authors, framework, principal theorems and experimental tasks. Text, equations, figures, tables and appendices support comparison, including matching material across renaming and relocation.

before.justification: V2 reports original MNIST and CIFAR-10 classification experiments and synthetic averaging experiments in Figure 1 and Appendix B.

after.justification: V3 reports original classification and averaging experiments on constructed and random communication graphs in Figure 1 and Appendix C.

M1.justification: The proposed F–RG update, clipping thresholds, momentum-SGD procedure and Spectral Heterogeneity attack remain unchanged. CSours is renamed CS+. The added weighting discussion and asynchronous analysis document choices and guarantees within the existing framework.

E1.justification: MNIST, CIFAR-10 and averaging tasks are retained. V3 additionally evaluates MNIST and averaging on randomly sampled Erdos-Renyi communication networks, substantially extending the tested environments beyond v2's constructed two-clique topology. The new averaging scenario also uses a common zero-centered Gaussian initialization instead of clique-dependent means.

E2.justification: V3 adds Iterative Outlier Scissors (IOS) to the reported classification and averaging comparisons. GTS–RG and the practical ClippedGossip comparator are retained; CSHe–RG is renamed ClippedGossip. The unattacked D-SGD reference remains in the CIFAR-10 comparisons.

E3.justification: MNIST heterogeneity changes from alpha=5 to 1. CIFAR-10 changes its reported budget from 2000 to 5000 iterations, honest graph from 26 nodes with k=8 to 16 with k=6, and stated CNN from four convolutional layers to three. Random-graph connectivity sweeps introduce new protocols. V3 contains unresolved discrepancies: CIFAR b=3 in Table 1 versus b=1 in Figures 4–5; random-graph MNIST has b=3 and T=300 in the table versus b=4 and T=200 in Figure 7.

E4.justification: Appendix C.2 adds a substantial robustness study varying random-graph connectivity under four attacks, measuring averaging error and MNIST loss/accuracy against algebraic connectivity. V2 primarily varied Byzantine weight on a fixed constructed graph. The new analysis directly tests sensitivity to network connectivity.

E5.justification: V2 reports five-seed means and min/max bands for MNIST; v3 specifies one seed and removes those uncertainty bands from the main comparison. Two-clique averaging changes from ten initializations to six seeds, retaining mean/min-max reporting. CIFAR-10 remains single-seed. Thus replication and uncertainty reporting change substantially for the central empirical evidence.

E6.justification: V3 replaces classification and averaging curves and adds IOS results, CIFAR-10 training-loss trajectories and random-graph results. For example, v2 Figure 3 shows CSours collapsing under FOE on CIFAR-10, whereas v3 Figure 5 shows CS+ retaining substantial accuracy. These use changed network, corruption and training settings, so they do not establish a same-setting performance improvement.

T1.justification: Corollary 4.7 becomes 4.8 and replaces summed gradient norms with time averages. Appendix G revises the stochastic-error dependence and explicitly includes the initial objective gap and honest-node count. Appendix A.1 adds a proof for the retained asynchronous proposition, extends omitted weight from exactly b to at most b, and states a rho+sqrt(rho) refinement. The main gossip and breakdown theorems remain unchanged. Corollary 4.8 also prints delta=2rho/mu2(GH), omitting the b factor used elsewhere.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction retain the framework, near-optimal clipping and spectral-attack contributions. The conclusion adds an explicit claim that experiments confirm the theory's ordering of existing methods' breakdown points, replacing v2's direct 'contrary to ours' contrast with methods failing before the optimal threshold.

C2.justification: Appendix A clarifies that relaxed synchrony still proceeds in rounds and explains how local weighting avoids requiring global spectral information. Remark B.1 adds why poorly designed attacks can misleadingly suggest trimming robustness. Appendix C.1 newly discusses training-loss instability that does not necessarily track test accuracy.

D1.justification: V3 adds detailed preprocessing instructions, layer-by-layer model descriptions, losses, batch sizes and momentum coefficients in Appendix B and Table 1. It explicitly describes the practical ClippedGossip threshold and IOS's use with momentum, and supplies an implementation repository link. These substantially expand reproducibility information, although the table/caption conflicts leave some settings unresolved.

R1.justification: V3 adds Hastings (1970) when discussing locally constructed graph weights. The principal positioning against earlier Byzantine learning methods remains intact. The adaptive-clipping reference changes title and publication metadata to its 2025 ICLR version, but the authors and ARC discussion identify it as the same previously cited work.

P1.justification: V3 renames CSours to CS+, makes experimental evaluation a separate Section 6, moves asynchronous discussion into Appendix A, and reorganizes experimental appendices by setup and graph family. It also expands the D-SGD explanation and adds acknowledgments. Most main-text exposition and existing proofs remain closely matched.

P2.justification: The empirical presentation is extensively revised: plots add IOS, reorder attack panels and change axis ranges; MNIST accuracy and loss are combined in Figure 3, redisplaying Figure 1's loss curves. V3 adds Table 1, CIFAR-10 loss plots and random-graph figures. The topology illustration is retained and renumbered from Figure 5 to Figure 8.

improvement.justification: V3 adds useful IOS and random-graph comparisons, substantially improves implementation documentation, and introduces time averaging in the D-SGD bounds. However, MNIST loses five-seed uncertainty reporting, Table 1 conflicts with experimental captions on corruption and budgets, and Corollary 4.8 introduces a corruption-parameter mismatch. These gains coexist with unresolved reliability problems in the revised evidence and theory, preventing a confident judgment of net overall improvement.
